title: Situations shared by every IT role
authored: Project-authored reflective scenarios (2026-10-23). Not a validated situational judgment test; there are no correct answers.

scenarios.title: Code review dispute
scenarios.prompt: A colleague's pull request works, but it introduces a pattern you think will make the module harder to maintain. They reply that it is a matter of taste and the deadline is tomorrow.

options.text: Approve it, add a follow-up ticket, and raise the pattern at the next team sync.
Request changes and explain clearly why the pattern will cost more later.
Ask a third engineer for a quick opinion before deciding.
Approve without comment; it is their code and the deadline matters more.

scenarios.title: 2 a.m. incident
scenarios.prompt: At 2 a.m. you are paged: checkout errors are rising. You recognise a likely cause, but the service belongs to another team whose on-call has not answered yet.

options.text: Roll back their last deploy yourself and post a detailed note in their channel.
Keep escalating to their on-call and manager while you gather evidence.
Apply a narrow mitigation you fully understand, such as a feature flag, and wait for them.
Open an incident bridge and hand coordination to the incident commander rota.

scenarios.title: Scope creep
scenarios.prompt: Halfway through a two-week piece of work, a stakeholder asks for 'one small addition' that you estimate would add four days.

options.text: Say no for now and offer to plan it as the next piece of work.
Agree and quietly absorb it by working longer hours.
Lay out the trade-off and let the stakeholder choose what to drop.
Build a rough version of the addition and see if it is enough.

scenarios.title: Estimate pressure
scenarios.prompt: You estimated a project at six weeks. A senior leader says it has to be three, because a partner announcement is planned.

options.text: Hold the six-week estimate and explain the specific risks of compressing it.
Propose a reduced scope that can genuinely ship in three weeks.
Commit to three weeks and figure out the details along the way.
Ask for two days to re-estimate with the team before answering.

scenarios.title: Tech debt or features
scenarios.prompt: The team keeps tripping over an old, fragile module. The roadmap for the next quarter is full of features.

options.text: Write a short proposal with the cost of the debt and ask for dedicated time.
Fix it in small steps inside feature work, without making it a separate project.
Leave the decision to whoever owns the roadmap and flag the risk once.
Ship the features and deal with the module when it actually breaks.

scenarios.title: Ambiguous requirements
scenarios.prompt: You receive a request that is one sentence long and can be read at least two different ways. The requester is busy this week.

options.text: Write down both interpretations and wait for an answer before starting.
Pick the more likely reading, build a small slice, and show it early.
Ask someone who knows the requester well and proceed from their read.
Build the version that covers both readings, even if it takes longer.

scenarios.title: Stakeholder escalation
scenarios.prompt: A stakeholder unhappy with a delay goes over your head to your manager with an inaccurate account of what happened.

options.text: Contact the stakeholder directly, correct the facts calmly and agree next steps.
Give your manager a factual timeline and let them handle the stakeholder.
Propose a joint meeting with the stakeholder and your manager to reset expectations.
Let it go and focus on finishing the work quickly.

scenarios.title: Build or buy
scenarios.prompt: Your team needs a feature-flag system. A paid service covers 90 percent of the need; building it in-house would take about a month.

options.text: Buy the service now and revisit if the missing 10 percent starts to hurt.
Run a structured comparison with a scoring matrix before deciding.
Build it; owning the core system is worth the month.
Trial the service for two weeks on one low-risk team first.

scenarios.title: Flaky tests before a release
scenarios.prompt: A release is due today. Two end-to-end tests fail intermittently, and nobody is sure whether they reveal a real bug.

options.text: Hold the release until someone understands the failures.
Release, watch the dashboards closely and keep a rollback ready.
Ask the test owners to decide whether it is safe.
Dig into the tests yourself for an hour, then decide.

scenarios.title: Adopting a new tool
scenarios.prompt: A new AI coding tool is getting attention. Some colleagues love it; others worry about quality and security.

options.text: Start using it on your own work right away and share what you learn.
Propose a small team pilot with agreed rules and a review date.
Wait until the security and legal questions are answered.
Try it privately on side projects before forming a view.

scenarios.title: Meetings or focus time
scenarios.prompt: Your calendar is filling with meetings and you have had no uninterrupted block for deep work in two weeks.

options.text: Block fixed focus time in your calendar and decline what conflicts with it.
Accept the meetings and do deep work early in the morning or late at night.
Ask meeting owners whether you are really needed, one by one.
Go with the flow; some weeks are like that.

scenarios.title: Your own mistake
scenarios.prompt: You realise a change you shipped last week has been silently corrupting a small share of records. Nobody else has noticed yet.

options.text: Announce it immediately to the team and affected owners, then start fixing.
Fix the bug and repair the data first, then explain what happened.
Tell your manager privately and agree together how to handle it.
Raise it with the data team so the repair is handled by the right experts.
